idiom_name: Stoplight(name, threshold:, cool_off_time:) with run, fallback and colour
implementation_notes: Stoplight is the in-process Ruby realization: Stoplight(name, window_size:, threshold:, cool_off_time:, recovery_threshold:) gives every dependency a traffic light whose run { } executes the block, whose run(fallback) { } serves a lambda while the light is red or yellow, and whose Stoplight::Error::RedLight carries light_name, cool_off_time and retry_after metadata; light.color exposes green/yellow/red for health checks, and the gem ships telemetry, data stores (in-memory, Redis) and an admin panel for manual lock/unlock. It replaces the classic hand-written flag with a colour state machine and needs no framework, so the hand-written form is only justified when the breaker must sit inside a driver (see the Semian variant) or when a single process's state is all that matters.
code_sketch:
PAYMENTS = Stoplight("payments", threshold: 3, cool_off_time: 30, recovery_threshold: 1)

receipt = PAYMENTS.run(->(error) { Receipt.degraded(error) }) do
  api.authorize(order)                 # yellow/red: the fallback runs instead
end

PAYMENTS.color                         # => "green" | "yellow" | "red"
PAYMENTS.lock(Stoplight::Color::RED)   # manual override for operations
pitfalls: The light is per process and per name: forked or multi-worker servers each keep their own colour unless a shared data store is configured, so the dependency sees N times the failing calls.
window_size defaults to nil, meaning errors are never aged out of the window, so a slow trickle of failures eventually turns the light red even if the recent past was healthy.
The fallback lambda runs whenever the light is not green (receiving nil in red state), so a fallback that calls the same dependency defeats the breaker.
Rescuing StandardError around run catches the RedLight short circuit together with genuine API errors and can hide which path produced the result.

variants.name: Semian driver-level breaker with cross-process coordination
variants.idiom_name: Semian resource adapters (tickets, error_threshold, error_timeout) raising driver-inherited errors
variants.implementation_notes: Semian protects the driver instead of the call site: adapters (mysql2, redis, net_http, activerecord_trilogy, activerecord_postgresql, postgres) are monkey-patched so that every connect or query first asks Semian whether the resource is available, coordinating through SysV semaphores in shared memory plus a shared store, and raising CircuitOpenError or ResourceBusyError which inherit from the driver's own base error class. Configuration sits where the client is created (name, tickets, success_threshold, error_threshold, error_timeout, open_circuit_on_oom and friends), so the breaker and the bulkhead are properties of the resource rather than of a block of application code. Choose it over Stoplight when the guarded unit is a database or Redis connection and the state must be visible to every forked worker; choose Stoplight when an arbitrary block of application code needs a breaker.
variants.code_sketch:
# Gemfile: gem 'semian', require: %w(semian semian/redis)

client = Redis.new(semian: {
  name: "inventory", tickets: 4, success_threshold: 2,
  error_threshold: 4, error_timeout: 20, open_circuit_on_oom: false,
})

begin
  client.get("stock:sku")
rescue Redis::BaseConnectionError => e     # also covers CircuitOpenError
  degraded_stock(e)
end
pitfalls: Coordination is server-wide through shared memory, so it does not span hosts: a fleet still builds one circuit per machine.
Adapters are opt-in through require, so a forgotten adapter silently leaves the resource unprotected even though the client was configured with semian options.
Semian's exceptions inherit from the driver's base error class, so rescuing a narrower driver error misses CircuitOpenError and the short circuit escapes as an unhandled exception.
Configuration is only validated strictly when force_config_validation is enabled; otherwise a mistyped threshold is logged and the breaker keeps its defaults.
